# Buoyancy and hydrostatics (`buoyancy_hydrostatics`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: helped by lever_mechanics_statics
- Core idea: A body in water is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces. So it floats if it is lighter than the same volume of water, and an iron ship floats if its hull encloses enough air. Weighing an object in air and again hanging in water gives its density and so detects alloyed gold: gold is 19.3 times as heavy as water, silver 10.5, lead 11.3, copper 8.9. Pressure in a liquid depends only on depth, not on the shape or width of the vessel (about one atmosphere per 10 m of water), and pressure applied to an enclosed liquid acts equally everywhere, which is the principle of the hydraulic press.
- Pitfalls:
  - Telling the crown story with the overflowing bath; the overflow is too small to measure, the practical method is the balance in water
  - Believing heavy things sink because they are heavy rather than dense
  - Thinking a wider water column presses harder at the bottom
  - Confusing displaced mass with volume: at the same load, a floating ship displaces the same mass but a smaller volume in salt water
- History: greece: c. 250 BC – Archimedes, On Floating Bodies; china: c. 200 AD – story of Cao Chong weighing an elephant by the sinking of a boat (Sanguozhi); islamic: 11th c. al-Biruni and 1121 al-Khazini measure specific gravities of metals and gems to about 1 per cent; europe: 1586 Galileo's little balance; 1586 Stevin's hydrostatic paradox; 1653 Pascal's treatise (published 1663); 1795 Bramah's hydraulic press
- Read:
  - Archimedes, On Floating Bodies (c. 250 BC)
  - Vitruvius, De architectura IX, preface
  - E. J. Dijksterhuis, Archimedes (1956)
